title: Suppressing an Alert Without Going Blind
context: Your SIEM generates 500 alerts per day. Analysts are overwhelmed and you must regain control of monitoring in three decisions.

n1.text: Before changing anything, what analysis do you conduct?

choices.text: Identify the rules producing the most false positives and understand their root cause
choices.why: Tuning must target noisy rules and understand why they are noisy.

choices.text: Disable all rules for one week
choices.why: You would lose all detection during that period.

choices.text: Hire more analysts to absorb the volume
choices.why: That treats the symptom, not the cause, and remains costly.

n2.text: A "failed login" rule alerts 200 times a day due to a known backup job. What do you do?

choices.text: Precisely exclude the backup account, document the exclusion, and set a review date
choices.why: Targeted exclusion removes noise without depriving the rule of its ability to detect real attacks.
Real brute-force attempts would no longer be detected.

choices.text: Ignore the alerts without written documentation
choices.why: Without documentation, no one can understand or reassess the choice later.

n3.text: You now want to see east-west communications between servers. Which source do you add?

choices.text: NetFlow/IPFIX complemented by port mirroring to the SIEM
choices.why: NetFlow reveals conversations and SPAN enables deeper inspection without disrupting traffic.
The perimeter firewall does not see internal server-to-server traffic.
Disabling correlation reduces detection instead of improving visibility.

n4.outcome: You reduced noise through targeted, documented tuning, then enriched collection with the right network telemetry.

debrief: Tuning relies on analyzing false positives, not blindly deleting rules.
An exclusion must be precise, documented, and periodically reviewed.
NetFlow and port mirroring provide visibility into internal traffic.
